1. Introduction to Jurassic English™ Level 1
1.1
Mission
Statement:
The
Genesis
of
Thought
At Level 1: Foundation, our mission is not the mastery of syntax, but the architecture of the internal world. For
learners aged 4–8, English is introduced not as a set of rules to be memorized, but as a high-precision tool for
"Excavating" human experience. We aim to move learners from passive reception to active Cognitive
Academic
Language
Proﬁciency
(CALP) by treating feelings as "Word Fossils" that carry objective intellectual
weight.
1.2
Pedagogical
Positioning:
The
Physiological
Precondition
Level 1 occupies a unique space in the Jurassic English™ (JE) ecosystem. While higher levels focus on
systemic critique and postcolonial satire, Level 1 focuses on the Physiological
Precondition
for
Reasoning.
We operate on the principle that a dysregulated nervous system cannot access the higher-order thinking
required for literary analysis. Therefore, Level 1 is a curriculum of "Regulated Reasoning."

1.4
Core
Cognitive
Progression:
From
Recall
to
Reasoning
The Foundation level initiates the vertical "Stratigraphy of Cognition" through a four-step evolutionary jump:
1. Sensation: Recognizing a physical feeling (Regulation).
2. Recall: Identifying the word associated with that feeling (Excavation).
3. Causality: Understanding the event that triggered the feeling (Strata).
4. Justiﬁcation: Explicitly linking the feeling to the event through evidence (Justiﬁcation).

Learning

Lesson 11: Excavation — Discovering Feeling Fossils in Owl
Babies
Target
Grade
Level
/
Subject
/
Duration
Grade
Level: Ages 4–8 (CEFR Pre-A1 →  A1)
Subject: English Language Arts (Jurassic English™ Level 1: Foundation)
Duration: 40 minutes
Overall
Learning
Goals
Students will transition into a regulated state of physiological readiness (the "Green Zone") to actively listen to a
weighty literary text about separation and wait time. They will excavate "Word Fossils" from the narrative —
vocabulary that captures the somatic experience of anxiety and the relief of return.
Speciﬁc
Learning
Objectives
1. Students will independently or semi-independently execute the "Butterﬂy Hug" self-regulation protocol to
achieve physiological readiness.
2. Students will identify and extract at least one speciﬁc "Word Fossil" (e.g., worried,
scared,
dark,
alone,
brave) from the read-aloud text.
3. Students will accurately connect their identiﬁed "Word Fossil" to a corresponding visual representation
(Emotion Icon or book illustration of Sarah, Percy, or Bill).
Materials
Needed
Core Text: Owl
Babies by Martin Waddell (physical book and/or audio-visual representation).
Emotion
Icons: Laminated cards featuring clear facial expressions or physical states (worried, scared,
alone, brave, relieved/happy).
Word
Wall
Materials: Blank cards, thick markers, and designated wall space.
Fidget
Fossils: Small, smooth stones provided for students requiring tactile neurodiverse accommodations.
Nature
Anchor: A visible natural object in the classroom — for this text, ideally a small branch or piece of
bark to evoke the owls' tree.

Detailed
Procedure
/
Step-by-Step
Outline
Phase
1:
Regulation-Before-Reasoning
(0–5
minutes)
Activity: The Butterﬂy Hug Protocol.
Teacher
Scripting
Prompt: "Paleontologists,
today
we
are
visiting
a
dark
forest
where
three
baby
owls
are
waiting.
Before
we
can
sit
with
them
in
the
dark,
we
must
get
our
brains
and
bodies
into
the
Green
Zone.
Cross
your
arms,
hook
your
thumbs,
and
tap
left,
right,
left,
right.
Breathe
quietly
with
me
for
60
seconds."
Student
Task: Students perform the Butterﬂy Hug, focusing on bilateral tapping and silent breathing to
regulate their autonomic nervous systems.
Action: Distribute "Fidget Fossils" to ADHD-proﬁle and high-anxiety students. Note: the Owl
Babies text is
emotionally activating for some children with separation anxiety — anchor objects are essential.
Phase
2:
The
Dig
Site
—
Active
Reading
(5–15
minutes)
Activity: Read-aloud of Owl
Babies.
Teacher
Scripting
Prompt: "Today,
we
are
looking
for
Word
Fossils
—
words
that
tell
us
how
the
three
baby
owls
feel
inside
their
bodies
while
they
wait
for
their
mother.
Listen
to
Sarah,
Percy,
and
little
Bill.
When
you
hear
a
feeling,
touch
your
nose."
Student
Task: Active listening. Students use the tactile gesture (touching nose) when identifying a target
word.
Action: Read the text slowly. Emphasize target BICS/CALP crossover vocabulary: worried,
scared,
dark,
alone,
brave,
soft. Pay particular attention to the smallest owl's repeated cry for his mother as the somatic
anchor for anxiety. Do not stop for grammar instruction.
Phase
3:
Excavation
—
The
Word
Fossil
Hunt
(15–30
minutes)
Activity: Identifying and claiming vocabulary.
Teacher
Scripting
Prompt: "Paleontologists,
what
Word
Fossils
did
we
ﬁnd
in
the
dark
layers
of
this
story?
What
words
tell
us
how
the
owls
felt
while
they
waited?"
Student
Task: Students verbally share a feeling word they noticed in the text.
Teacher
Move
(Marking): When a student says "Worried" or "Scared," the teacher executes the
Accountable Talk "Marking" move: "You
found
a
fossil.
'Worried'
is
what
your
tummy
feels
when
you
don't
know
if
someone
is
coming
back.
Let's
put
that
on
our
Word
Wall." Write the word clearly on a card and
place it on the board.
Action: Continue until 3–4 key feeling words are "excavated" and placed on the Word Wall. Aim for at least
one Tier 2 fossil (e.g., worried or brave) beyond the basic sad/happy.
Phase
4:
Linguistic
Connection
&
UDL
Expression
(30–35
minutes)
Activity: Connecting text to visual evidence (A1 Indicator prep).
Teacher
Scripting
Prompt: "I
am
holding
up
a
picture
of
little
Bill
on
the
branch,
calling
out
for
his
mother.
Which
Word
Fossil
from
our
wall
matches
Bill's
face
and
body?"
Student
Task: Students point to or verbally identify the correct Word Fossil (e.g., "Worried" or "Scared")
that matches the provided Emotion Icon or book illustration.

Diﬀerentiation
/
Accommodations
Neuroinclusive
(ADHD): Provide a "Fidget Fossil" to hold during the 40-minute thinking block. Allow
standing during Phase 3 if the student remains engaged in the "hunt."
Neuroinclusive
(Anxiety): Owl
Babies may activate students with separation anxiety. Use the "Safe Start"
— the teacher models the ﬁrst Excavation. Have a quiet "Regulation Station" nearby in case a student
needs a longer reset. Never cold-call an anxious student during the Word Hunt.
Support
Tier: Provide students with pre-selected feeling cards with pictures (worried face, brave face) on
their desks. They can hold up the picture card when they hear the matching word.
Core
Tier: Students must provide a spoken Claim plus visual evidence (e.g., pointing at the book and
saying, "Bill is scared").
Extension
Tier: Prompt advanced reasoning: "Which
baby
owl
feels
the
MOST
worried?
How
can
we
tell
from
the
picture?" (Students may notice Bill's smaller size, his repeated lines, or his position on the branch.)

Homework
/
Extension
Activities
Home
Connection: "Internal Fossil Hunt." Students are tasked with noticing one time they feel "worried" or
"brave" at home this evening, and must tell their parent/guardian which "Word Fossil" they are feeling.
Extension: parents may share their own answer to model that adults feel these fossils too.
